title: Why Trust May Be the Real Bottleneck at Work – T.C.
summary: Businesses everywhere are under pressure. More complexity, more tools, more “best practices” piling up and somehow, things feel heavier than ever. But what if HR and leadership more broadly could feel lighter? What if instead of chasing endless checklists, we focused on just two meta skills that make everything else easier? That’s the vision shared by Susan Chen
body_markdown:
## Start With the Feeling


T.C. brought one question from advertising into the way he designs each session. What should people feel when it ends? An HR team will usually begin with the activity, the schedule and the learning objectives. T.C. begins with the response he wants from the room.


Should people feel more comfortable speaking in front of each other? Should two departments be less guarded? Should new managers feel able to lead without pretending to know everything? The answer affects who performs together, how the session is introduced and what happens after the song. It also gives HR a clearer way to choose an activity. A team that rarely speaks across departments needs a different session from a group learning to present to clients.


## Playing and Performing


T.C. also separates playing a song from performing it. A musician can hit every note correctly and still leave the audience cold. A performer understands what the song is saying and makes the audience believe it.


He sees the same difference in the workplace. Someone can read every slide without holding the room. A manager can repeat the company values without showing them in practice. A CEO can deliver the approved message while sounding disconnected from it. People notice when someone is only going through the material. They also notice when the person speaking means it.


## What Should Still Be Different on Monday?


Teams can have an enjoyable afternoon and return to the same habits the next morning. T.C. asks companies to decide what they expect to change after the activity. If the purpose is simply to let employees have fun, that is a valid reason. If the company expects better teamwork, it needs to be more specific.


Perhaps two managers need to speak without involving a third person. Perhaps employees need to ask questions earlier. Perhaps senior leaders need to become easier to approach. The activity should give people a chance to practise that behaviour while they are together. Otherwise, the company has organised entertainment and called it development.
